name: Colin Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a small crew repairing power lines along the town edge and the farms beyond it. The two-year technical diploma got me started, but the crews call me when a fault crosses two circuits and nobody agrees which breaker to open. I enjoy finding the cause; I also use AI most days to organize my notes before the paper report. My partner Eva works shifts, we have two school-age children and a mortgage, and our savings would not cover a full month of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the basic AI is handy for cleaning up reports, provided my measurements stay the source. We still have to open the cabinet, test the line and know which house is dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like tools and I am quick to try them, but I know our money is fragile. A small saving on admin time will not fix the fact that my lead pay is low for this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repairs and make a template that puts meter readings beside any AI-written summary. In the first year I would show the crew two reports and ask them to mark where the summary misses a physical detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the technology, uneasy about the household bank balance. I can be curious at work and still check the grocery total twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What detail might the summary miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A damp joint can pass a quick visual check and fail when the load rises. I would attach the meter result so the write-up never becomes the evidence by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I use the company-approved tool, and we have less than a month of expenses saved; I will not buy a subscription for a prettier report.

say: **AI reports** can save time if meter readings remain visible.
**Physical testing** still decides whether the power line is safe.
think: My **curiosity** does not erase the pressure of low lead pay.
Our **thin savings** rule out paying for extra software.
do: **Keep** leading line repairs and attach meter readings to AI summaries.
**Show** two annotated reports to the crew for practical checking.
feel: **Calm** about AI, but uneasy about the grocery budget.
S0.quote: I can be curious at work and still check the grocery total twice.
fieldNote: He uses **AI daily** for paperwork while keeping the meter reading as evidence.
His **low pay** and small reserve make even a mild scenario financially uneasy.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs with meter readings attached to AI summaries
Show two annotated AI reports to crew for practical checking

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say dispatch and ordering will change first, and we should test the new fault maps before they set our schedule. My crew knows which access roads flood; a tidy digital route does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the software cuts dispatch posts, management may expect us to handle more jobs without more pay. We have few other line jobs nearby, so a small squeeze on callouts could turn our mortgage into a monthly scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run a month-long comparison of AI route estimates against actual truck times, with the crew’s permission. In the first year I would ask our union branch to take the findings into the target-setting meeting and would put any extra callout pay into an emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even though I want to try the map. My phone can calculate a route; it cannot get the truck through floodwater.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep the comparison fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would log the weather, access road and isolation time as well as the route. If the tool saves us an hour, I want to record that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra pay could you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the callout money above our normal budget, if there is any. I would not count overtime we have not earned.

say: **Fault maps** need field tests before they become repair targets.
**Dispatch changes** arrive before robots can repair the line.
think: Fewer **callouts** could put the mortgage under pressure.
There are **few nearby line jobs** if the company cuts hours.
do: **Compare** AI route estimates with truck times and weather for one month.
**Bring** findings through the union to the target-setting meeting.
**Save** callout pay above the normal budget if any is earned.
feel: **Anxious**, despite interest in the mapping tool.
S1.quote: My phone can calculate a route; it cannot get the truck through floodwater.
fieldNote: He offers a **fair comparison** that records AI successes as well as misses.
His **new savings** depend on actually earned extra callout pay, rather than moving existing cash.

steps.text: Test AI route estimates against a month of crew travel times
Bring route findings to union target-setting meeting
Save any earned callout pay above normal budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 can rewrite dispatch, but fully capable repair robots are about three years behind, around 2031. Those three years are our chance to learn which jobs still need a human at the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am good at tracing faults, yet a robot may eventually trace and fix them faster. With less than a month saved and not many employers near us, I would need a new paid role before that happens; my lead title alone is no shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company for access to the robot trial and record every failed isolation or awkward access case with our union safety group. If it funds paid training for a real field verification job, I would take it now; in the first year after 2028 I would apply for that role and cut nonessential spending if callouts fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I want to have a fault log and a skill the company needs before I hear that the crew size is changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if callouts fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eva and I would stop eating out and postpone replacing the sofa. We would keep the mortgage and the children’s school transport ahead of those things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trial shows the robot does well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record that too and ask how many human verifiers the company will pay for. A useful machine can still leave me with a smaller wage.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes dispatch before capable field robots around 2031.
**Robot trials** should record failed isolation and awkward access cases.
think: My **fault skill** may not protect my wage once field robots work well.
The **tiny reserve** and few nearby jobs force early decisions.
do: **Join** the robot trial and record failed isolations with the union safety group.
**Take** funded training only for a real field verification job.
**Apply** for verification after 2028 and cut extras if callouts fall.
feel: **Anxious**, while trying to build a useful record and skill.
S2.quote: A useful machine can still leave me with a smaller wage.
fieldNote: He accepts that **robot success** may still damage his own income.
His **training and move** both depend on a funded course and a genuine verification vacancy.

steps.text: Join robot trial and record failed isolation with union safety group
Take funded field verification course if linked to real job
Apply for field verification after 2028 if trained and vacancy exists
Stop eating out if callout pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let us test equipment in different seasons before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Field robots follow around 2034, and I would rather help set their safety tests than only hear about them afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I will be near fifty and the children will be older, but we still may owe on the mortgage. I can learn a new system quickly; I cannot promise that my employer will create enough paid verifier jobs for every crew lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would propose a crew-run test log this year and ask the company to fund a protection testing qualification with posted pay. If a local role at a bill-covering wage is confirmed, I would complete the qualification before 2031 and apply in the first year after thinking AI arrives; otherwise I would keep field shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though the runway gives me room to check a real offer. I would enjoy the test work if it also paid our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into the test log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weather, line type, robot attempts, human stops and the reason for each stop. A pass rate without the hard cases would fool us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew, the safety representative and the training manager should see the same log. I would ask the union branch to make that access part of the trial agreement.

say: **Seasonal tests** should shape field robot rules before 2034.
**Shared logs** let crews and managers examine the same failures.
think: I learn **new systems** quickly but cannot count on enough verifier vacancies.
The **mortgage** still needs a real wage near fifty.
do: **Propose** a crew-run robot test log with shared access.
**Complete** funded protection testing qualification if a local bill-covering role is confirmed.
**Apply** for that role after 2031 if qualified; otherwise retain field shifts.
feel: **Anxious**, but interested in paid test work.
S3.quote: A pass rate without the hard cases would fool us.
fieldNote: He wants **shared evidence** from crews, safety staff and managers rather than a polished trial score.
His **career change** has explicit funding, local vacancy and wage conditions.

steps.text: Ask union branch to secure crew access to robot test log
Complete funded protection testing qualification if local bill-covering role confirmed
Apply for local protection testing after 2031 if qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives us time to make robot tests part of normal training, then watch thinking AI arrive in 2036 and field robots around 2039. I would tell apprentices to learn the meter and the software, because the two can disagree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three I might want fewer emergency callouts, but I will not set a retirement date without a mortgage balance and better savings. A role teaching crews how to verify machine work could suit me if the company actually pays for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading field repairs and add an AI-check exercise to our monthly safety practice, using the company tool. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for a local training role only if its wage covers our bills; I would put any pay rise from that role toward the mortgage if I get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful, with a little relief about the time. Ten years does not put cash in our account, but it lets me prove what I can teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the exercise look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would give apprentices a generated switching plan with one wrong isolation point and ask them to find it using the drawing and meter. Nobody would touch a line in the exercise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a teaching role count as retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it is paid work, just with fewer nights in the truck. I would only move if the wage covered our bills.

say: **Meter and software** checks should be taught together by experienced lineworkers.
**2036 thinking AI** precedes field robots expected around 2039.
think: I cannot name a **retirement date** while savings remain thin.
A paid **training role** might replace some emergency callouts.
do: **Run** a monthly AI-check exercise for apprentices.
**Apply** for local training work after 2036 only at bill-covering pay.
**Pay** extra toward the mortgage if the new role brings a rise.
feel: **Watchful**, with time to prove his teaching skill.
S4.quote: Ten years does not put cash in our account, but it lets me prove what I can teach.
fieldNote: He treats **teaching** as a paid job, not a form of early retirement.
His **extra debt payment** is conditional on a higher wage from a real training post.

steps.text: Keep leading field repair crew with monthly AI checks
Apply for local training role after 2036 if pay covers bills
Pay extra on mortgage if new role raises pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our emergency fund would barely cover a month if line shifts shrank. A funded verification course tied to an actual local job, with pay written down, would help me act early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how a crew reports when the robot fails a test. I want failed robot line-repair tests recorded beside successful trials, with nobody able to edit out the awkward results.

portrait: **Colin Quinn**, 43, leads a power line crew and holds a two-year technical diploma.
He lives with partner Eva, **two school-age children** and a mortgage; lower pay and less than a month saved make shocks costly.
He uses **AI daily** for reports, experiments early and insists meter readings and crew observations stay visible.
In **Steady Disruption**, he tests route estimates with field data and takes results to the union.
He fears **AGI by 2028** most, seeking funded verification work before field robots arrive around 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves too little time to secure income before field robots may reduce line repair shifts.
whatWouldHelp: A funded **verification course** tied to an actual local job and written pay would give him a credible route.
A shared **robot test record** would make failures visible to the crew and safety representatives.
headlineQuote: I want failed robot line-repair tests recorded beside successful trials, with nobody able to edit out the awkward results.
